children: Sprouts Farmers Market operates specialty grocery stores focused on fresh, natural and organic food across the United States. The company ended its most recent quarter with 504 stores in 25 states, built around a produce-centric layout and a growing private label program.

For several years, Sprouts was one of the best stories in food retail. Its health-and-wellness positioning attracted a loyal, higher-income customer, its smaller-format stores generated strong returns, and steady comparable sales growth paired with an aggressive opening schedule earned the stock a premium multiple.

That story has broken down in 2026. Traffic is falling, the customer is migrating toward value retailers, and management has concluded that the only way to win shoppers back is to invest heavily in price. That may well be the right strategic call, but it comes at a direct cost to margins, and the earnings outlook is being reset accordingly.
The Zacks Rundown

Sprouts has been underperforming the market badly. A Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), the stock has fallen roughly 41% year to date and recently traded under $50, registering a 52-week low. Shares collapsed roughly 23% in a single session following the third-quarter report on October 29th.

The company is part of the Zacks Food – Natural Foods Products industry group, which currently ranks in the bottom 6% out of approximately 250 industries. Because this industry is ranked in the bottom half of all Zacks Ranked Industries, we expect it to underperform the market over the next 3 to 6 months, just as it has over the past year:

While individual stocks have the ability to outperform even when included in weak industries, their industry association serves as a headwind for any potential rallies. Stocks in this group are also expected to post below-average earnings growth. With much better alternatives in the current market environment, this stock should be avoided.
Traffic Is the Problem

Sprouts reported third-quarter results that missed on both lines. Earnings of $1.21 per share came in just below the $1.22 Zacks Consensus Estimate and slipped from the year-ago quarter, while revenue of $2.30 billion grew 4.7% but fell about 1% short of expectations. Revenue growth came entirely from new stores, with a record 15 openings in the quarter.

The underlying store base went backward. Comparable store sales fell 0.9%, as comparable transactions dropped 3.3% and were only partially offset by a 2.5% increase in average basket size. Management said comps softened through August and September and did not recover as year-over-year comparisons eased, a detail that argues against a temporary disruption.

Margins compressed across the board. Gross margin fell 50 basis points to 38.2% on higher shrink and elevated fuel costs, while EBIT margin declined roughly 60 basis points to 6.6% and operating income fell 2.9%. Management noted that weakness is concentrated among less-engaged, somewhat lower-income customers, but also acknowledged modest softening among its core shoppers — the customers Sprouts can least afford to lose.

The guidance reset is where the real damage was done. Full-year comparable sales are now expected to decline about 1.7%, down from a prior range of negative 0.5% to positive 0.5%. Net sales growth was cut to about 4.3% from 5.5% to 6.5%, and earnings guidance fell to about $4.80 per share from $5.32 to $5.40.
Deteriorating Forecasts

Analysts have been slashing their numbers. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for 2026 has fallen 10.81% over the prior 60 days to $4.95 per share, while the 2027 consensus dropped nearly 30% to $4.12 — a projected decline of nearly 17% from this year.

Some on the Street are already further along. BofA Securities downgraded the stock to Underperform and cut its 2027 estimate to $3.90 from $5.90, while RBC moved to Sector Perform and characterized the sales weakness as company-specific rather than cyclical. Stifel, initiating with a Hold, estimates the January price reset will cost more than $100 million and expects EBIT margin to settle in the low 5% range.
Missing expectations, cutting guidance and watching forward estimates fall across every period is a recipe for stock price underperformance. These are exactly the trends that the bears like to see.
Technical Outlook

SFM SFM stock is in a well-defined downtrend. Shares gapped sharply lower on the October report and have spent the weeks since trading near their lows rather than recovering any of the lost ground. Both the 50-day (blue line) and 200-day (red line) moving averages are sloping downward, and the stock sits well beneath each of them.
Image Source: StockCharts
Shares would need to reclaim both moving averages and show a genuine turn in earnings estimate revisions to warrant taking any long positions in the stock.
Final Thoughts
Whole Foods is growing in overlapping markets, and conventional grocers have spent years expanding their natural and organic assortments. Sprouts is cutting prices into a fight it no longer controls.

Leadership is also in transition. President and COO Nick Konat takes over as CEO on January 4th, the same month the national pricing strategy launches, with Jack Sinclair moving to executive chairman. A new CEO inheriting a margin reset and a February guidance call is not a setup that typically produces upside surprises.

None of this is an indictment of the brand. Sprouts has a differentiated format, a strong private label and a new-store engine that still produces high returns. But a deteriorating fundamental and technical backdrop, membership in a weak industry group, and falling future earnings estimates will likely serve as a ceiling on any potential rallies.
